newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing juror differs with death penalty.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing juror differs with death penalty.

text.p: A lawyer questioned as a potential juror in the Oklahoma City bombing case Thursday said she feared being confronted with the question of a vote for capital punishment.
"I don't know if I would ever sleep again," the 80th prospective juror said. "To me, you become the executioner."
District Court Judge Richard Matsch was understanding, saying "your answers tell me this is something you have struggled with in your mind and probably in your soul."
The judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys have quizzed 86 jury candidates for 14 days on a number of issues including the death penalty. Eight jurors were questioned on Thursday.

Another potential woman juror said point blank she could not vote for the death penalty because she does not consider it a punishment. "The punishment would be for him to have to stay alive ... If he's alive and working he's going to feel it," she said.

But most of those quizzed so far have said they could vote to execute defendant Timothy McVeigh if he is found guilty of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.
McVeigh was attentive during the jury questioning. Dressed in a burgundy coloured shirt, with sleeves neatly rolled up, he made notes and conferred with his attorneys.

To be among the 12 jurors or six alternates, potential jurors must be able to say they can consider all alternatives during sentencing if McVeigh is convicted. If jurors are totally opposed to the death penalty or believe it is the only punishment they could vote for, they would be excluded.
A jury is expected to be selected by next week and once that step is completed, attorneys on both sides will have to restrict their performances to the courtroom.
Matsch Wednesday issued a written gag order reiterating his earlier directive that all parties in the case refrain from making statements outside the courtroom.

The jury will not be sequestered and the judge wants to make sure they are not exposed to comments from lawyers outside the courtroom. McVeigh's chief attorney, Stephen Jones, Thursday took out a handkerchief outside the courthouse and jokingly put it over his mouth when asked by reporters about the gag order.

Security remained tight around the federal complex in downtown Denver that includes the courthouse as Saturday's anniversaries of the Oklahoma bombing and the 1993 siege at the Branch Davidian complex near Waco, Texas, approached.
Observances of the bombing anniversary are expected to be low key. A Catholic church in downtown Denver will ring its bells 168 times, once for each victim of the bombing.
